name: service-stub
intent: Let a client depend on the contract of a remote service while a local stand-in answers its calls, so client code can be built and tested without the real service and the remote dependency sits behind one replaceable seam.
problem: A client depends on a third-party or remote service that is out of the team's control: not deployed yet, rate-limited, metered per call, unreliable, or simply unreachable from the test environment. Client work stalls and the tests either cannot run or become slow and flaky, so the development process breaks exactly where the remote boundary is (the catalog trigger: the client needs a stand-in for a remote service - also for tests).
context: Applies at any boundary where a client's own logic must be exercised independently of the remote counterpart: enterprise systems integrating credit scoring, tax lookups or pricing engines; clients written against a contract that has no implementation yet (IDL- or OpenAPI-first development); RPC stacks where a generated client stub is the only handle on the remote; and test suites that need deterministic answers, scripted failures or fully offline execution.
benefits: Client development and CI continue while the remote service is absent, rate-limited, metered, flaky or not yet released: the stand-in runs locally, in memory and fast.
Tests become deterministic - no network, no credentials, no third-party quotas, no dependence on someone else's uptime or latency.
Failure and edge paths become producible on demand: timeouts, 5xx, partial or malformed payloads, expired tokens, retries - all things a healthy remote service will not emit for you.
The remote dependency turns into an explicit, injectable seam, so the real implementation can be swapped back in without touching client logic.
Parallel development: the client is written and compiled against the contract before the service exists, and with generated stubs a contract mismatch surfaces at build time instead of in production.
The expensive, network-bound path leaves the inner development loop and is exercised deliberately instead of on every unit test run.
RPC toolchains push the same idea into production: the generated stub is a local object with the service's methods, so client code never touches marshalling or the channel.
tradeoffs: Contract drift is silent: the stand-in encodes what the client believes the remote does, so tests stay green after the remote contract changed and the failure appears in production.

False confidence by construction: serialization, transport, authentication, retry policy and the remote's own validation never execute against a stand-in, so a passing suite proves only that the client is consistent with its own fiction.
Maintenance multiplies: the contract, the real client, the stand-in and its fixture data all track the same interface, and every contract change lands in several places.
Over-specified stand-ins are brittle: expectations that pin call order, argument identity or call counts fail on refactors that change no behaviour.
Permissive stand-ins hide error handling: one that answers anything with a default means the validation, timeout and error branches are never exercised.
A stand-in can reach production: wired by a feature flag, a configuration default or a leftover factory fallback, it keeps the system looking healthy while serving invented data.
Generated production stubs add a codegen step and version-lock the client to the IDL, so contract evolution requires regeneration and coordinated releases.

participants.responsibility: Depends only on the service contract and behaves the same whether it holds the remote implementation or the stand-in.
The interface the client holds: operations, types and error semantics of the remote service, expressed in the client's own terms.
Local implementation of the contract that answers from canned or scripted data, fast and in memory, without touching the network.
The production counterpart - generated client stub bound to a channel, gateway, or hand-written remote client - which the stand-in must remain substitutable for.
Decides which implementation the client receives: constructor injection, DI container, factory or plugin, build/link configuration, or the RPC runtime that binds a generated stub to a channel.
Keeps the stand-in honest: the published IDL or OpenAPI document, recorded real interactions, or contract tests that replay the same expectations against the live service.

use_cases: A client for an integration partner that is unavailable in the development environment (credit scoring, tax rate lookup, pricing engine) is built, demoed and reviewed against a local stand-in.
Unit and integration tests of client logic that must not touch the network: canned answers, deterministic timing, no credentials, no vendor quotas.
Reproducing failure handling - timeouts, 5xx responses, malformed or partial payloads, expired tokens - that the live service cannot be asked to produce on demand.
Offline and air-gapped development or demos where the remote service is unreachable by design.
RPC-style development in which the client is written against a stub generated from the IDL before any server exists, and the same client is later pointed at a real endpoint.

Consumer-driven contract testing with Pact: the consumer's expectations run against Pact's mock provider, the resulting pact file is replayed against the real provider, which is what keeps stand-in and service from drifting apart.

gRPC clients are built on protoc-generated stubs (e.g. RouteGuideGrpc.java's blockingStub/asyncStub, Go's generated client): the client is written and compiled against the .proto before any server exists, then the same stub is bound to a real channel.

SDK-first vendor integrations: teams compile against client stubs generated from a published OpenAPI document by OpenAPI Generator, so partner work starts on the day the spec lands instead of the day the vendor's SDK does.
avoid_when: The dependency can be run locally without effort (embedded server, container, in-process transport): run the real thing - a stand-in here only hides an avoidable setup cost.
The purpose of the test is the integration itself: verify it with contract tests or against a sandbox, because a stand-in cannot fail the way the remote fails.

What you need to check is the wire contract - format, headers, status handling, retry and timeout behaviour: intercept at the network layer (MSW, WireMock, WebMock, responses) instead of substituting the client's collaborator.
You do not own the interface: wrap it behind your own contract or record real interactions rather than hand-maintaining a stand-in for a foreign SDK you cannot keep in sync.
The client is thin glue over the vendor's client library: an end-to-end smoke test against a sandbox is cheaper than a parallel implementation nobody maintains.
The work is a throwaway script or spike: call the service directly and delete the code afterwards.
anti_patterns: Stand-in in production: a stub left wired by a feature flag, configuration default or factory fallback that serves invented data while monitoring stays green.
Stub drift by memory: a hand-written stand-in updated from the client's calls instead of the remote contract, with no contract test to catch the divergence.
Mocking what you do not own, layer by layer, so the suite pins your own invented protocol rather than the vendor's real one.
Interaction over-specification: verifying exact call sequences, argument objects and counts, so any refactor of the client fails although its behaviour is unchanged.
Permissive stand-ins (relaxed mocks, lenient fakes, mocks without a spec) that answer anything, so validation and error branches never execute.
Real customer payloads copied into the stand-in's fixtures, turning a test artefact into a data-protection incident.
design_principles: Dependency inversion: the client depends on the remote contract, not on the transport or the vendor's client type.
Liskov substitution: the stand-in must honour the same pre- and postconditions as the real implementation, otherwise it is a different contract wearing the same name.
Single responsibility for the seam: only the composition root decides which implementation is used; the client never branches on it.
Interface segregation: the stand-in implements the view of the service the client actually uses, not the whole remote API.
Fail fast: a stand-in that answers unexpected calls silently is less safe than one that fails them, because the failure it hides belongs to the remote.
best_practices: Derive the stand-in from the published contract (IDL, OpenAPI, recorded interactions) and keep it in the test tree, never in a shippable path; a build configuration is safer than a runtime flag.
Make the stand-in strict: fail on unexpected operations, arguments and counts, and require every canned answer to be declared.
Protect against drift with contract tests that replay the same expectations against the real service (consumer-driven contracts), and re-record fixtures when the contract changes.
Model the remote's failure modes - timeouts, error codes, partial and malformed payloads - not just the happy path.
Keep fixture data representative and sanitized; prefer captured-and-redacted payloads over invented ones.

Choose the seam deliberately: interface-level stand-ins for client logic, network-level interception when the wire contract itself must be exercised, generated stubs when an IDL is the source of truth.
Keep the seam in one place (composition root, DI registration, factory) so switching implementations is a configuration change and never a code fork.
Review production wiring for leftover stand-ins and delete doubles that no longer correspond to a live contract as part of release readiness.
sources: Fowler, Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture (2002), Base Patterns chapter 18 - Service Stub: replace a problematic remote service with a local, fast, in-memory implementation, typically behind a Gateway.
Meszaros, xUnit Test Patterns (2007) - Stub / Test Double: the family of in-process stand-ins this pattern's test face belongs to.
